_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine -- California rule seed, 2026-08-24. Loaded through add_rule.
Every provision below was read VERBATIM from the California Legislature's own
site (leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) or the Judicial Council's own rules site
(courts.ca.gov) before being encoded.
TWO COMPUTATION STANDARDS, NOT ONE. This is the thing about California that a
blanket standard would get wrong on roughly half these rows:
ca_ccp_12_12a  for a period fixed by STATUTE -- CCP 12, 12a, 12b, 12c.
Used by every civil-litigation row here, because each of
those periods comes from the Code of Civil Procedure.
ca_crc_1_10    for a period fixed by the RULES OF COURT -- Cal. R. Ct. 1.10.
Used by the appellate rows, because Rule 8.104 is a rule of
court, not a statute.
The two produce the same arithmetic today. That is precisely why one standard
is tempting and wrong: the audit trail has to name the authority that actually
governs the deadline in front of the attorney, and the two can diverge on
amendment. CCP 12a(b) does sweep broadly ('whether expressed in this or any
other code or statute, ordinance, rule, or regulation'), but Rule 1.10 exists
separately and says so in its own words for rules-based periods.
NO ENGINE CHANGE WAS NEEDED -- and that was VERIFIED, not assumed. The same
prediction was made for Florida and was wrong there (2.514(a)(1)(A) shifts the
start of the count), so it was carried forward as unverified and then checked
against the text: CCP 12 excludes the first day and includes the last, with no
short-period exclusion and no shifted start, and Rule 1.10(a) says the same in
different words. Both map to the existing frcp_6a implementation.
THE 60/60/180 APPEAL PROBLEM -- READ THIS BEFORE TRUSTING AN APPELLATE DATE.
Cal. R. Ct. 8.104(a)(1) requires a notice of appeal on or before the EARLIEST
of three alternatives, each running from a different event and two of them
with a different period. They are encoded as three separate rows because they
are three different clocks. THE ENGINE COMPUTES EACH ONE INDIVIDUALLY AND DOES
NOT TAKE THE EARLIEST FOR YOU -- it cannot, unless it is given all three
trigger dates, and in most matters only some of the three events have
happened. A California appellant must compute every applicable row and use the
earliest result. Relying on a single row can produce a date LATER than the
true deadline, which is the one direction that loses an appeal.
THE UNLAWFUL DETAINER FIVE-DAY VARIANTS are encoded as their own rows.
CCP 2030.260(b), 2031.260(b) and 2033.250(b) each give a five-day period in an
unlawful detainer action or other proceeding under Chapter 4 (commencing with
Section 1159). Whether a matter is an unlawful detainer is a case fact the
engine has no field for, so it never chooses between the 30-day row and the
five-day one -- same treatment as Michigan's in-state/out-of-state service
rows and Florida's 45-day defendant alternatives. Note the two production and
admission variants say 'at least five days', a floor, while the interrogatory
one says 'five days' flat; that difference is preserved in the notes.
SERVICE EXTENSIONS: THE AMOUNT DEPENDS ON THE METHOD, AND ON FACTS THE ENGINE
CANNOT SEE. CCP 1013(a) extends a period after service by MAIL by 5 calendar
days if both the place of mailing and the place of address are within
California, 10 if either is outside California but within the United States,
12 if the address is the Secretary of State's address confidentiality program,
and 20 if either is outside the United States. CCP 1013(c) (Express Mail or
other overnight delivery), CCP 1013(e) (facsimile, permitted only by written
agreement) and CCP 1010.6(a)(3)(B) (electronic) each extend by TWO COURT DAYS.
Court days are not calendar days. Two court days across a weekend is four
calendar days and across a holiday weekend more, so counting them as calendar
days would produce a date EARLIER than the true deadline. The engine counts
them properly.
A BARE 'mail' SERVICE METHOD IS DELIBERATELY REJECTED. Callers must supply one
of mail_within_california, mail_outside_california_within_us,
mail_to_address_confidentiality_program or mail_outside_us. Defaulting to the
in-state five would be wrong by 5, 7 or 15 days whenever the guess is wrong,
and a service extension that is silently too short is the dangerous direction.
THE APPELLATE ROWS CARRY NO EXTENSION, AND THAT IS THE LAW, NOT AN OMISSION.
Both CCP 1013 and CCP 1010.6(a)(3)(B) say the extension 'shall not apply to
extend the time for filing' a notice of intention to move for new trial, a
notice of intention to move to vacate judgment under Section 663a, or A NOTICE
OF APPEAL. All three Rule 8.104 rows are notices of appeal.
NOT ENCODED, deliberately, and flagged rather than dropped:
1. CCP 12b, the office-closed limb: 'If any city, county, state, or public
office, other than a branch office, is closed for the whole of any day ...
that day shall be considered as a holiday for the purposes of computing
time under Sections 12 and 12a.' Unknowable in advance. Same class as
Indiana's T.R. 6(A) limb, Illinois's Governor-proclamation limb and
Florida's chief-justice hurricane limb.
2. The Judicial Council's discretionary power under CCP 135 to designate an
alternative observance day when a judicial holiday falls on a weekend.
'May', not 'shall' -- so no automatic shift is applied. See the calendar.
3. Gov. Code 6700(a)(20) days appointed by the GOVERNOR. CCP 135 carves out
presidentially appointed days but not gubernatorial ones, so those are
real judicial holidays and are genuinely unknowable in advance.
4. Every 'unless on motion ... the court has shortened/extended the time'
clause in the discovery statutes, and Cal. R. Ct. 1.10(c)'s general power
to extend or shorten. A court order displaces these dates and the engine
cannot see one.
5. NOTHING about the service extensions -- they ARE now encoded. Added
2026-08-24 after reading CCP 1013 and 1010.6 verbatim; an earlier version
of this file said they were unread and unattached, which was true then and
is not now. See SERVICE EXTENSIONS below.
6. Cal. R. Ct. 8.108, which EXTENDS the time to appeal when certain
post-trial motions are filed, and rules 8.702/8.712. 8.104(a)(1) opens
'Unless a statute or rules 8.108, 8.702, or 8.712 provides otherwise' --
so a matter with a post-trial motion must not rely on these rows alone.
7. CCP 412.20(a)(3)'s 'Except as otherwise required by statute' opening.
A different statute can set a different response period.

rules.label: Written pleading in response to the complaint after service of summons (California)

service_extension.note: Amount and unit come from the standard, not this row: CCP 1013(a) adds 5, 10, 12 or 20 CALENDAR days for mail depending on the places of mailing and address, and CCP 1013(c)/(e) and 1010.6(a)(3)(B) each add 2 COURT days. Supply the specific service_method -- a bare "mail" is deliberately not accepted, because the amount depends on facts this engine cannot see.

authority.quote: A direction that the defendant file with the court a written pleading in response to the complaint within 30 days after summons is served on the defendant.
authority.note: The 30 days is prescribed as CONTENT OF THE SUMMONS rather than as a free-standing deadline -- 412.20(a) lists what a summons must contain, and (a)(3) is the direction it must carry. The practical deadline is the same, and the section opens 'Except as otherwise required by statute', so another statute can displace it. Statutory period, so the statutory computation standard applies (CCP 12/12a), not Rule 1.10. Service extensions under CCP 1013/1010.6 ARE attached; supply a specific service_method (see the file readme).

service_extension.note: Amount and unit come from the standard, not this row: CCP 1013(a) adds 5, 10, 12 or 20 CALENDAR days for mail depending on the places of mailing and address, and CCP 1013(c)/(e) and 1010.6(a)(3)(B) each add 2 COURT days. Supply the specific service_method -- a bare "mail" is deliberately not accepted, because the amount depends on facts this engine cannot see.

authority.quote: Within 30 days after service of interrogatories, the party to whom the interrogatories are propounded shall serve the original of the response to them on the propounding party, unless on motion of the propounding party the court has shortened the time for response, or unless on motion of the responding party the court has extended the time for response.
authority.note: The unlawful detainer variant in 2030.260(b) is a separate row. Both the shortening and the extending clause are court-order escapes the engine cannot see. effective_from is the effective date of the amendment quoted (Stats. 2007, Ch. 113, Sec. 8, effective January 1, 2008).

rules.label: Response to interrogatories in an unlawful detainer action (California)

service_extension.note: Amount and unit come from the standard, not this row: CCP 1013(a) adds 5, 10, 12 or 20 CALENDAR days for mail depending on the places of mailing and address, and CCP 1013(c)/(e) and 1010.6(a)(3)(B) each add 2 COURT days. Supply the specific service_method -- a bare "mail" is deliberately not accepted, because the amount depends on facts this engine cannot see.

authority.quote: Notwithstanding subdivision (a), in an unlawful detainer action or other proceeding under Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 1159) of Title 3 of Part 3, the party to whom the interrogatories are propounded shall have five days from the date of service to respond, unless on motion of the propounding party the court has shortened the time for response, or unless on motion of the responding party the court has extended the time for response.
authority.note: Its own row because whether a matter is an unlawful detainer is a case fact the engine has no field for and must never guess. Note the wording is a FLAT five days here -- 'shall have five days' -- where the production and admission equivalents say 'at least five days'. That difference is real and is preserved rather than normalised. California has NO short-period exclusion, so a five-day period counts straight through weekends and rolls only if the last day lands on one.

rules.label: Response to a demand for inspection, copying, testing or sampling (California)

service_extension.note: Amount and unit come from the standard, not this row: CCP 1013(a) adds 5, 10, 12 or 20 CALENDAR days for mail depending on the places of mailing and address, and CCP 1013(c)/(e) and 1010.6(a)(3)(B) each add 2 COURT days. Supply the specific service_method -- a bare "mail" is deliberately not accepted, because the amount depends on facts this engine cannot see.

authority.quote: Within 30 days after service of a demand for inspection, copying, testing, or sampling, the party to whom the demand is directed shall serve the original of the response to it on the party making the demand, and a copy of the response on all other parties who have appeared in the action, unless on motion of the party making the demand, the court has shortened the time for response, or unless on motion of the party to whom the demand has been directed, the court has extended the time for response.
authority.note: California calls this a DEMAND for inspection, not a request for production -- the trigger_event uses California's own term rather than the label other jurisdictions in this engine use, so a caller cannot select it by accident from a neighbouring state's vocabulary. The unlawful detainer variant in 2031.260(b) is a separate row. effective_from is the effective date of the amendment quoted (Stats. 2009, Ch. 5, Sec. 15, effective June 29, 2009).

rules.label: Response to a demand for inspection in an unlawful detainer action (California)

service_extension.note: Amount and unit come from the standard, not this row: CCP 1013(a) adds 5, 10, 12 or 20 CALENDAR days for mail depending on the places of mailing and address, and CCP 1013(c)/(e) and 1010.6(a)(3)(B) each add 2 COURT days. Supply the specific service_method -- a bare "mail" is deliberately not accepted, because the amount depends on facts this engine cannot see.

authority.quote: Notwithstanding subdivision (a), in an unlawful detainer action or other proceeding under Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 1159) of Title 3 of Part 3, the party to whom a demand for inspection, copying, testing, or sampling is directed shall have at least five days from the date of service of the demand to respond, unless on motion of the party making the demand, the court has shortened the time for the response, or unless on motion of the party to whom the demand has been directed, the court has extended the time for response.
authority.note: 'AT LEAST five days' -- a FLOOR, not a fixed period, unlike the interrogatory variant's flat 'five days'. The date this produces is therefore the earliest a response could be due, not necessarily the date it is due. Same shape as Illinois's Rule 214(a) and Ohio's Civ.R. 34(B) minimum-period rules.

service_extension.note: Amount and unit come from the standard, not this row: CCP 1013(a) adds 5, 10, 12 or 20 CALENDAR days for mail depending on the places of mailing and address, and CCP 1013(c)/(e) and 1010.6(a)(3)(B) each add 2 COURT days. Supply the specific service_method -- a bare "mail" is deliberately not accepted, because the amount depends on facts this engine cannot see.

authority.quote: Within 30 days after service of requests for admission, the party to whom the requests are directed shall serve the original of the response to them on the requesting party, and a copy of the response on all other parties who have appeared, unless on motion of the requesting party the court has shortened the time for response, or unless on motion of the responding party the court has extended the time for response.
authority.note: IMPORTANT DIFFERENCE FROM ILLINOIS AND FLORIDA: 2033.250 does NOT itself deem the matters admitted on default. California's deemed-admitted consequence runs through a separate motion under CCP 2033.280, which is not encoded here. So missing this date is serious but is not self-executing the way Ill. S. Ct. R. 216(c) and Fla. R. Civ. P. 1.370(a)(6) are. The unlawful detainer variant in 2033.250(b) is a separate row.

rules.label: Response to requests for admission in an unlawful detainer action (California)

service_extension.note: Amount and unit come from the standard, not this row: CCP 1013(a) adds 5, 10, 12 or 20 CALENDAR days for mail depending on the places of mailing and address, and CCP 1013(c)/(e) and 1010.6(a)(3)(B) each add 2 COURT days. Supply the specific service_method -- a bare "mail" is deliberately not accepted, because the amount depends on facts this engine cannot see.

authority.quote: Notwithstanding subdivision (a), in an unlawful detainer action or other proceeding under Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 1159) of Title 3 of Part 3, the party to whom the request is directed shall have at least five days from the date of service to respond, unless on motion of the requesting party the court has shortened the time for response, or unless on motion of the responding party the court has extended the time for response.
authority.note: 'AT LEAST five days' -- a floor, like the inspection-demand variant and unlike the interrogatory one. The date produced is the earliest a response could be due.

rules.label: Notice of appeal, 60 days from the clerk's service of notice of entry (California)

trigger_document.label: the date the superior court CLERK served a document entitled Notice of Entry, or a filed-endorsed copy of the judgment showing the date it was served
trigger_document.not_the: the date the judgment was entered, or the date a PARTY served notice -- Cal. R. Ct. 8.104(a)(1) makes those three separate limbs with three different dates

authority.quote: 60 days after the superior court clerk serves on the party filing the notice of appeal a document entitled 'Notice of Entry' of judgment or a filed-endorsed copy of the judgment
authority.note: ONE OF THREE ALTERNATIVES, AND THE DEADLINE IS THE EARLIEST OF THEM. 8.104(a)(1) requires the notice on or before the earliest of (A), (B) and (C); this engine computes each individually and does NOT take the earliest, because it is not given all three trigger dates. Compute every applicable row and use the earliest. Relying on this row alone can produce a date LATER than the true deadline. A RULE of court, so the rules-of-court computation standard applies (Cal. R. Ct. 1.10), not CCP 12/12a. NOT encoded: rule 8.108, which extends the time when certain post-trial motions are filed, and rules 8.702/8.712 -- 8.104(a)(1) is expressly subject to all three. NO SERVICE EXTENSION, by law: CCP 1013 and CCP 1010.6(a)(3)(B) both exclude a notice of appeal from the extension in terms.

rules.label: Notice of appeal, 60 days from a party's service of notice of entry (California)

trigger_document.label: the date a PARTY served, or was served with, a document entitled Notice of Entry of judgment, or a filed-endorsed copy of the judgment
trigger_document.not_the: the date the judgment was entered, or the date the CLERK served notice -- those are the other two limbs of Cal. R. Ct. 8.104(a)(1) and they bear different dates

authority.quote: 60 days after the party filing the notice of appeal serves or is served by a party with a document entitled 'Notice of Entry' of judgment or a filed-endorsed copy of the judgment, accompanied by proof of service
authority.note: The second of the three alternatives -- see the (A) row's note on taking the earliest. Distinct from (A) in WHO served: the clerk in (A), a party in (B). Both can happen in one matter, on different dates, and each starts its own 60 days. The rule requires proof of service accompanying the document for this limb to bite. NO SERVICE EXTENSION, by law: CCP 1013 and CCP 1010.6(a)(3)(B) both exclude a notice of appeal from the extension in terms.

rules.label: Notice of appeal, 180-day outside limit from entry of judgment (California)

trigger_document.label: the date the clerk ENTERED the order or judgment on the docket
trigger_document.not_the: the date it was signed, decided, announced in court, or mailed to the parties -- those are different events and they bear different dates

authority.note: The outside limit, and the only one of the three that always runs -- entry of judgment always happens, while service of a notice of entry may not. It is a CEILING, not the deadline: if either 60-day limb has been triggered, the earliest controls and this date is irrelevant. Per 8.104(a)(3), where the parties stipulated to waive notice under CCP 1019.5, this limb applies unless the court or a party serves notice of entry to start (A) or (B). NO SERVICE EXTENSION, by law: CCP 1013 and CCP 1010.6(a)(3)(B) both exclude a notice of appeal from the extension in terms.
